previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for an acute flare of chronic pancreatitis with severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and her standard IV pain and anti-nausea regimen. During the admission, she developed a fever, and blood cultures grew Herbaspirillum species, a gram-negative rod likely originating from her port. She was treated with IV antibiotics, initially Zosyn and then switched to ceftazidime based on sensitivities, with concurrent antibiotic dwells into the port. Her pain improved, and she was advanced to a regular diet. Her anemia was addressed with IV iron, and anticoagulation was managed with a Lovenox bridge back to warfarin. She was discharged home with home health services to complete a course of IV ceftazidime and port dwells, along with instructions for INR monitoring and follow-up blood cultures.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo female with history of CFTR mutation and chronic 
pancreatitis with history of ~40 admissions over past several 
years, including most recently ___, presenting with 
abdominal pain similar to prior episodes, likely pancreatitis 
flare with steady improvement in pain, nausea, and vomiting over 
admission.  Course also complicated by Herbaspirillium line 
sepsis

# Bacteremia:  Pt with found to grow Herbaspirillium species in 
her line cultures during her prior admission.  She was treated 
with ceftazidime for a 14 day course which was due to be 
completed on the day of presentation of current admission.  We 
initially continued her on Ceftazidime, but blood cultures 
obtained on the day of admission were significant for persistent 
Herbaspirillum.  ID was consulted who recommended switching 
zosyn for a 14 day course.  It should also be noted that patient 
had a portacath which had been placed several weeks earlier 
given her poor peripheral access and frequent need for IV 
therapy in the hospital, and there was concern that this was the 
source of her persistent bacteremia.  After discussions with ID 
and the patient, the decision was reached to pull the portocath 
in place of a temporary CVL to allow her to continue her IVF and 
pain medications throughout admission.  She remained afebrile 
throughout admission, and all subsequent daily blood cultures 
were negative.  Her central line was pulled on discharge, and 
she was sent home on a PO ciprofloxacin regimen of 500mg q12h to 
complete her ___hronic pancreatitis:  Pt has had ~40 admissions over the past 
several years for acute on chronic pancreatitis, most recently 
from ___.  She presented on this admission with her normal 
midepigastric pain with radiation to the back along with nausea 
and vomitting. ___ score was 0.  She has been well known to 
the ___ system and upon each admission she has been placed on 
an aggressive pain/antiemetic regimen of:

-Dilaudid 8mg IV Q2hrs (hang  w/ 50cc bag NS and infuse over 
15min), 
-Ketorolac 15mg IV Q6hrs 
-Ondansetron 4mg IV Q8hrs (hang w/50cc bag NS and infuse over 
15min)
-Phenergan 25 mg IV Q4hrs (hang w/ 50cc bag NS and infuse over 
15min)
-Compazine 10mg IV q4h
-Lorazepam 0.5mg IV Q4hrs Lorazepam 1 mg qhs. 
-D5W ___ at 125 cc/hr

The patient has grown a tremendous tolerance to high-dose 
opiods.  As an outpatient, she is also on dilaudid 8mg PO q3h 
prn, but the patient uses the dilaudid around the clock 
regularly.  However, given the patient's chronic flares, a 
proper detox would be very difficult to pursue.  A 
multidisciplinary meeting was held to address this issue, and 
the patient's PCP and outpatient gastroenterologist were made 
aware of her current admission.  The decision was ultimately 
made to pursue a formal outpatient pain management consultation 
which the patient will set up.  She appears very motivated to do 
this.  In terms of her acute flare, she was maintained on the 
above regimen and was able to slowly advance her diet with 
improvement in her nausea, vomiting and pain.  She was eating a 
regular diet on discharge.  She was sent home on her regular 
outpatient PO medication which includes PO dilaudid (8mg q3h 
prn), methadone, and promethazine.  PO compazine was also added 
on discharge to help further control her nausea.

# History of LUE DVT: Pt with history of LUE DVT first diagnosed 
in ___. This has been treated as an outpatient with various 
regimens of lovenox and coumadin.  During her prior admission, 
she was taken off of her coumadin and started on lovenox 
in-house given her NPO status and concern for poor absorption 
during her acute flare.  Upon discharge, she was restarted on 
coumadin with anticoagulation follow up.  Upon presentation this 
admission, her INR was supratherpeutic at 4.1.  Anticoagulation 
was held and her INR trended down.  She was started on lovenox 
once INR dropped below 2.0, and eventually bridged back to 
coumadin once she was tolerating PO.  Coumadin dose varied 
day-to-day from ___, and was held on ___ as INR was 
supratherapeutic again at 3.8.  On the day of discharge she was 
subtherapeutic down to 1.8, so she was given a dose of lovenox 
prior to discharge and instructed to take 7.5mg of coumadin 
daily with an INR check on ___ to be faxed to her PCP.   

# Anemia: Pt is chronically anemic with recent baselines in the 
mid-high ___.  Hct was 30.6 admission, but subsequently trended 
down and stabilized in the mid-20s throughout most of the 
admission.  She has h/o Fe-deficiency anemia which has been 
treated with IV iron in the past, however iron studies were 
checked this admission and were within normal limits.   It is 
very likely that this is a manifestation of her chronic disease 
state.

# Leukopenia:  WBC trended down to 2.9 on ___ from 6.0 on 
admission.  Her diff was checked and was normal.  We attributed 
this to her antibiotics.  By discharge WBC was stable at 4.0. 

# HTN:  BPs  were often elevated in-house, likely a combination 
of pain and inconsistent absorption of her PO lisinopril.  SBPs 
often reached 150s-160s over most of the admission.  We 
increased her lisinopril dose to 20mg daily (from 10mg) and her 
pressures were improved to 120s-130s on discharge. 

# Diarrhea:  Pt noted to have on/off watery diarrhea throughout 
most of the admission.  Given her recent antibiotics, C. Diff 
toxin was sent and negative.  This very well could be a 
non-infectious antibiotic associated diarrhea further 
complicated by her abdominal pain from her pancreatitis flare.  
By discharge, diarrhea had improved and became less frequent.
 
# Access: Upon discharge, patient has no peripheral access as 
her portacath was removed during this admission due to her 
bacteremia.  She is a very difficult stick for peripheral access 
but we explained to the patient that the risk of persistent 
bacteremia was too high to keep her line in.  She understood 
this and agreed to the removal.  The issue of access will 
certainly become an issue during future admissions, and we feel 
that temporary lines would be best.

# Follow up:
- Pt to follow up with PCP, ___, and pain management.  We feel 
that an opiate detox would be the ideal option, but acknowledge 
the difficulty of doing this with her frequent flares.  We hope 
that a pain management consult will helpful for this. 
- As above, peripheral access will remain an ongoing issue
- We insisted that the patient see her primary 
gastroenterologist as she has not seen him in follow-up 
(in-person) for over a year now.
